html:
The big picture

Every object in Analysis lives in a set: the domain of a function, the solutions of an inequality, an interval, \mathbb{R} itself. A set is fixed by one thing only, which objects are its elements, so every statement about sets is really a statement "x \in A" that is true or false. That turns set theory into the logic of chapter 1 in disguise. A subset A \subseteq B is the implication x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B, and two sets are equal when each is a subset of the other. The operations complement, intersection, union, difference and symmetric difference are \neg, \wedge, \vee, "and not" and "exactly one", and the laws of set algebra (De Morgan, distributive …) are the laws of logic, proved the same way: take an arbitrary element and follow the logic. Sizes are measured by cardinality; the power set collects all subsets, and infinite sets come in two sizes, countable and uncountable. The Cartesian product builds ordered pairs and so describes all combinations of choices, from the plane \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} to a robot's configuration space. Sets are always taken from a universal set: Russell's paradox shows what goes wrong if you allow "the set of all sets with property P".

Connection

The Math prep course introduced the notation and drew the operations as Venn diagrams: 1 Mathematical Thinking and Preliminaries (sections Sets: definition & notation and Set operations (visual)). New here: equality and subsets as logical statements, cardinality and the power set, countability, the full algebra of sets with elementwise proofs, and the Cartesian product.

What can we do with collections?

Set theory gives us a precise way to speak about objects, membership, restrictions, and combinations.

DescribeCompareCombine
x \in A, x \notin AA \subseteq B, A = BA \cap B, A \cup B, A \setminus B
What belongs to the collection?How are two collections related?How do we build new sets?

The logic from last time reappears as membership logic.

Where sets appear again

Robotics, AI, and engineering

  • state spaces and configuration spaces;
  • feasible sets in optimization;
  • classes, labels, and datasets in machine learning;
  • events in probability and stochastics;
  • database queries and filtering conditions.

In this course

  • domains and ranges of functions;
  • intervals and neighborhoods;
  • solution sets of equations and inequalities;
  • sets of real numbers: bounds, max/min, sup/inf.

We use only basic set theory, but we use it constantly.

What is a set?

A set is a well-defined collection of objects. The objects are called elements or members.

Examples: \{1, 2, 3\}; the set of all integers; all students in this room; all solutions of x^2 = 1.

Well-defined means:

  • membership is not ambiguous;
  • for an object x, the statement x \in A is either true or false.

\{1, 2, 3\} = \{3, 1, 2, 2\} — order and repetitions do not matter.

Board. \mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\} = \{k : k \text{ is a positive integer}\}, \mathbb{Z} = \{\ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots\}. So 1 \in \mathbb{N}, -2 \notin \mathbb{N}, 1 \in \mathbb{Z}, \frac12 \notin \mathbb{Z}. Sets do not remember order or repetition: A = \{1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3\} = \{1, 2, 3\} = \{3, 2, 1\}, and \lvert A \rvert = 3.

Intuition

A set is a bag that answers exactly one kind of question: "is this thing in you, yes or no?" It doesn't know an order, and it doesn't count copies. For each object x, "x \in A" is a proposition in the sense of 1 Elements of Logic: true or false, nothing in between. "All tall students in this room" is not well-defined, because "tall" has no yes/no answer.

Basic notation

NotationMeaning
A, B, X, Ysets
a, b, x, yelements
a \in Aa is an element of A
a \notin Aa is not an element of A
A = \{a, b, c, \ldots\}set given by listing
\emptysetempty set
Uuniversal set under discussion

Slide picture: A = \{a, b, c\} drawn as a circle with the three points inside, so a \in A and d \notin A.

Board. In the lecture the universal set was written V: the set all elements of the current context are taken from (e.g. \mathbb{R} when we talk about real numbers). The slides call it U; this note uses U from here on.

Board: the empty set

\emptyset is the set with no elements. Example:

\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 0\} = \emptyset
Symbols
  • \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 0\} — the set of all real numbers x whose square is negative (read ":" as "such that")
  • \mathbb{R} — the real numbers; \emptyset — the empty set
Intuition

x^2 \ge 0 for every real x, so no real number qualifies. Differently described empty sets are all the same set: \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 0\} = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : n < 0\} = \emptyset, because sets with the same elements (here: none) are equal. That's why it is called the empty set.

Board: Russell's paradox

Why you can't call every collection a set:

R = \{A : A \notin A\}, \qquad R \in R\,?
Symbols
  • R — the collection of all sets A that are not elements of themselves
  • \{A : \ldots\} — "the collection of all A such that …" (set-builder notation)
  • A \notin A — "A is not an element of A"
  • R \in R\,? — the question that breaks it: is R an element of itself?
Why is this a paradox?

Ask whether R \in R and use the definition of R in both cases.

  1. Suppose R \in R. Every element of R satisfies "not an element of itself", so R \notin R. Contradiction.
  2. Suppose R \notin R. Then R satisfies the membership condition, so R \in R. Contradiction.

So "R \in R" can be neither true nor false, which a proposition must be. The way out: R is not a set — it isn't well-defined. You may not form a set from any property over "all sets"; you only collect elements from a set you already have, \{x \in U : P(x)\}. That's why every definition in this chapter starts with "Let A \subseteq U".

Intuition

The everyday version: a village barber shaves exactly those men who don't shave themselves. Who shaves the barber? Either answer contradicts the rule. The conclusion isn't that barbers are impossible, it's that such a barber can't exist, just as such a set can't.

Special sets of numbers

The number systems as nested sets: \mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{C} (slide 6).

\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{C}
Symbols
  • \mathbb{N} — natural numbers \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\} (this course starts at 1; see the convention warning in 3 Set of Real Numbers)
  • \mathbb{Z} — integers; \mathbb{Q} — rational numbers (fractions \frac{p}{q}, q \ne 0); \mathbb{R} — real numbers; \mathbb{C} — complex numbers
  • \subseteq — "is a subset of" (next section)
Connection

Why each of these sets is needed (each solves equations the previous one can't) is the topic of 3 Set of Real Numbers for \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R} and 4 Complex Numbers for \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{C}.

Subsets

A set A is a subset of B, written A \subseteq B, if every element of A is also an element of B.

A \subseteq B \iff \forall x\, (x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B)
Symbols
  • A \subseteq B — "A is a subset of B"; \iff — "means exactly", "if and only if"
  • \forall x — "for every object x"; \Rightarrow — implication from 1 Elements of Logic

If A \subseteq B and A \neq B, then A is a proper subset: A \subsetneq B.

Slide picture: circle A drawn inside circle B. Board example: \{1, 2\} \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}, and it is a proper subset.

Quick check. \emptyset \subseteq A? A \subseteq A? — Yes, both are true.

Intuition

A \subseteq B is an implication with a quantifier, so it is checked like one: go through the elements of A and look for one that is missing from B. One missing element (a counterexample, 1 Elements of Logic › Witnesses and counterexamples) makes it false; if none is missing, it is true.

Why are \emptyset \subseteq A and A \subseteq A true for every set A?
  • \emptyset \subseteq A means \forall x: (x \in \emptyset \Rightarrow x \in A). The premise x \in \emptyset is false for every x, and an implication with a false premise is true (1 Elements of Logic › Implication when the hypothesis is false). So it holds for every x, whatever A is. In words: \emptyset has no element that could be missing from A.
  • A \subseteq A means \forall x: (x \in A \Rightarrow x \in A), and P \Rightarrow P is a tautology.

So "subset" allows equality; that is why the strict version needs its own symbol \subsetneq.

Common mistake — \in versus \subseteq

1 \in \{1, 2\} (1 is an element), but "1 \subseteq \{1, 2\}" is meaningless, because 1 is not a set. Conversely \{1\} \subseteq \{1, 2\} (the set containing 1 is a subset), but \{1\} \notin \{1, 2\}: the elements of \{1, 2\} are the numbers 1 and 2, not the set \{1\}. Rule: on the left of \in stands an element, on both sides of \subseteq stand sets.

Equality, cardinality, and power set

Equality

A = B \iff A \subseteq B \text{ and } B \subseteq A
Symbols
  • A = B — the sets have exactly the same elements
  • A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A — "each set is contained in the other" (the two inclusions)
Why don't order and repetition matter?

A set only records membership: "is 1 in it? is 2 in it?" \{1, 2\}, \{2, 1\} and \{1, 1, 1, 2\} give the same answers to every such question, so each is a subset of the others and they are equal. Listing 1 three times doesn't make 1 "more" of an element. When order or repetition does matter, mathematics uses other objects: ordered pairs and tuples (1, 2) \neq (2, 1) (see the Cartesian product below), or lists in Python.

Worked example — proving two sets equal by both inclusions

Claim: \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 = 1\} = \{-1, 1\}.

  1. Show \subseteq: take any x with x^2 = 1. Then (x - 1)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 1 or x = -1; thus x \in \{-1, 1\}.
  2. Show \supseteq: 1^2 = 1 and (-1)^2 = 1, so both elements of \{-1, 1\} satisfy the condition.
  3. Conclude: each set is a subset of the other, so they are equal. This "both inclusions" pattern is the set version of proving \Leftrightarrow by proving both directions.

Cardinality

For finite sets, the cardinality \lvert A \rvert = number of elements of A. Example: \lvert \{2, 4, 7\} \rvert = 3.

Quick check. \lvert \{1, \{1\}, \emptyset\} \rvert = ? — Answer: \lvert \{1, \{1\}, \emptyset\} \rvert = 3.

Common mistake — a set inside a set is one element

Tempting: "\{1, \{1\}, \emptyset\} has 2 elements, because \{1\} is just 1 again and \emptyset is nothing." But the number 1 and the set \{1\} are different objects, and \emptyset written inside braces is an element like any other. So there are three elements: 1, \{1\}, \emptyset. Same trap: \lvert \emptyset \rvert = 0 but \lvert \{\emptyset\} \rvert = 1 — an empty bag versus a bag containing an empty bag.

Special types

  • \emptyset: empty set (0 elements);
  • \{a\}: singleton (1 element);
  • finite / infinite;
  • countable / uncountable.

Board. A finite set: \lvert A \rvert is finite. An infinite set: infinitely many elements. Infinite sets can be countable or uncountable. A countable set: its elements can be put in one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. Example:

A = \{1, 4, 9, 16, \ldots\} = \{n^2 : n \in \mathbb{N}\}
Symbols
  • \{n^2 : n \in \mathbb{N}\} — the set of all squares of natural numbers (each element is n^2 for some n \in \mathbb{N})

is countable: 1 \leftrightarrow 1, 4 \leftrightarrow 2, 9 \leftrightarrow 3, … But B = (0, 1) = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : 0 < x < 1\} is uncountable.

Intuition

Countable = "can be written as an endless list a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots that eventually reaches every element". The squares can: list them in order. Even \mathbb{Z} can, by zig-zagging 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, \ldots. (Here "countable" is used for infinite sets, as on the board; many books also call finite sets countable.)

Why can't (0, 1) be listed? (Cantor's diagonal argument)

Suppose some list x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots contained every number in (0, 1). Write each in decimal: x_1 = 0.\mathbf{d_{11}}d_{12}d_{13}\ldots, x_2 = 0.d_{21}\mathbf{d_{22}}d_{23}\ldots, and so on. Build a new number y = 0.e_1e_2e_3\ldots by changing the diagonal digits: e_k = 5 if d_{kk} \neq 5, and e_k = 4 if d_{kk} = 5. Then y \in (0, 1), but y differs from x_k in the k-th digit, so y \neq x_k for every k: y is missing from the list. Contradiction, so no complete list exists. (Using only the digits 4 and 5 avoids the 0.4999\ldots = 0.5 double-representation issue.) This is a proof by contradiction, as in 1 Elements of Logic › Proof by contradiction.

Power set

The power set of A is the set of all its subsets:

\mathcal{P}(A) = \{B : B \subseteq A\}
Symbols
  • \mathcal{P}(A) — the power set of A: the set whose elements are all the subsets of A
  • B — a subset of A (here B is just a name for "any subset", not a fixed set)

If A = \{a, b\}, then \mathcal{P}(A) = \{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a, b\}\}.

Board. For finite A, \lvert \mathcal{P}(A) \rvert = 2^{\lvert A \rvert}. Example: if A = \{1, 2, 3\}, then

\mathcal{P}(A) = \{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{1, 2\}, \{1, 3\}, \{2, 3\}, \{1, 2, 3\}\}
Symbols
  • symbols as above; \lvert \mathcal{P}(A) \rvert — the number of subsets of A

So \lvert \mathcal{P}(A) \rvert = 8 = 2^3.

Why does a set with n elements have 2^n subsets?

Building a subset means making one yes/no decision per element: "is this element in B or not?" For A = \{1, 2, 3\} that is three independent decisions with 2 options each, 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8 ways, and every way gives a different subset (all "no" gives \emptyset, all "yes" gives A). In general 2^n. It is the same count as the rows of a truth table with n propositions.

Operations mirror logic

LogicSet operationMembership statement
not Pcomplement A^cx \in A^c \iff x \notin A
P and Qintersection A \cap Bx \in A \cap B \iff x \in A \wedge x \in B
P or Qunion A \cup Bx \in A \cup B \iff x \in A \vee x \in B
P and not Qdifference A \setminus Bx \in A \setminus B \iff x \in A \wedge x \notin B

Venn diagrams visualize membership truth values. Read every set operation as a statement about an arbitrary element x.

Intuition — the membership table

Since everything depends only on the truth values of "x \in A" and "x \in B", a truth table over those two statements is a complete description of every operation. Each row is one region of the Venn diagram:

x \in Ax \in BA \cap BA \cup BA \setminus BA \triangle B
TTTTFF
TFFTTT
FTFTFT
FFFFFF

Two set expressions are equal exactly when their columns agree in every row — the set version of a truth-table check for \Leftrightarrow. The A \triangle B column is the XOR column A \oplus B from 1 Elements of Logic.

Complement

Let A \subseteq U. The complement of A in U is

A^c = \{x \in U : x \notin A\}
Symbols
  • U — the universal set under discussion; A \subseteq U
  • A^c — the complement of A: everything in U that is not in A

The complement A^c: the shaded part of U outside A (slide 10).

Example. U = \mathbb{Z}, A = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}. Then A^c = \{\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0\}.

Board example. If U = \mathbb{R} and A = (0, 1), then A^c = (-\infty, 0] \cup [1, \infty).

Common mistake — a complement without its universal set

Tempting: "A^c is simply everything that isn't in A." But "everything" has to be fixed first — that is exactly what Russell's paradox forbids leaving open. The complement depends on U: for A = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\} the slide gets A^c = \{\ldots, -1, 0\} in U = \mathbb{Z}, but in U = \mathbb{N} the same A has A^c = \emptyset, and in U = \mathbb{R} it contains every non-integer too. Always read A^c as "complement in U".

Intersection and union

Intersection (common elements) and union (at least one set):

A \cap B = \{x \in U : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}, \qquad A \cup B = \{x \in U : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}
Symbols
  • A, B \subseteq U — two sets in the universal set U
  • A \cap B — intersection ("A and B"); A \cup B — union ("A or B", inclusive or: elements in both count)

Left: A \cap B, the overlap. Right: A \cup B, both circles (slide 11).

Example: \{1, 2, 3\} \cap \{1, 2, 5\} = \{1, 2\}, \{1, 2, 3\} \cup \{1, 2, 5\} = \{1, 2, 3, 5\}.

Difference and symmetric difference

Difference and symmetric difference:

A \setminus B = \{x \in U : x \in A \text{ and } x \notin B\}, \qquad A \triangle B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A) = (A \cup B) \setminus (A \cap B)
Symbols
  • A \setminus B — "A without B": the elements of A that are not in B
  • A \triangle B — symmetric difference: the elements in exactly one of the two sets

Left: A \setminus B, the part of A outside B. Right: A \triangle B, both circles without the overlap (slide 12).

Board. Interpretation of A \triangle B: in exactly one of the two sets.

Quick check

Let A = \{1, 2, 3\}, B = \{1, 2, 5\}. Compute A \cap B, A \cup B, A \setminus B, B \setminus A, A \triangle B.

Solution (slide): A \cap B = \{1, 2\}, A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 5\}, A \setminus B = \{3\}, B \setminus A = \{5\}, A \triangle B = \{3, 5\}.

Connection

Python's set type has the same operations, so you can check finite examples in Programming 1: {1, 2, 3} & {1, 2, 5} gives {1, 2}, | is union, - is difference and ^ is symmetric difference ({3, 5}). x in A is the membership test x \in A.

Algebra of sets: basic laws

Let A, B, C \subseteq U.

Idempotent: A \cup A = A, A \cap A = A.

Commutative: A \cup B = B \cup A, A \cap B = B \cap A.

Associative: A \cup (B \cup C) = (A \cup B) \cup C, A \cap (B \cap C) = (A \cap B) \cap C.

Identity and domination: A \cup \emptyset = A, A \cap U = A, A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset, A \cup U = U.

Distributive:

A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C), \qquad A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)
Symbols
  • A, B, C \subseteq U — any three sets in the universal set U; \cap intersection, \cup union
Connection

Each law is a law of propositional logic from 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic with \wedge \to \cap, \vee \to \cup, true \to U, false \to \emptyset: the distributive laws here are the ones in 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws. Exercise sheet 1 (Problem 1.4b) asks for the proof of the first distributive law; see Exercise Sheet 1 – Solutions.

Complement laws and De Morgan's laws

Let A, B \subseteq U.

Complement laws: A \cap A^c = \emptyset, A \cup A^c = U, U^c = \emptyset, \emptyset^c = U, (A^c)^c = A.

De Morgan's laws:

(A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c, \qquad (A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c
Symbols
  • A, B \subseteq U; (\ldots)^c — complement in U of the set in brackets

These are the set versions of \neg(P \wedge Q) \iff \neg P \vee \neg Q and \neg(P \vee Q) \iff \neg P \wedge \neg Q.

Intuition

"Not in both" means "missing from at least one": x \notin A \cap B exactly when x \notin A or x \notin B. Taking the complement swaps \cap and \cup, just as negation swaps \wedge and \vee (and \forall and \exists).

Difference and symmetric difference: useful identities

Difference:

  • A \setminus B = A \cap B^c
  • A \setminus A = \emptyset, A \setminus \emptyset = A
  • \emptyset \setminus A = \emptyset, U \setminus A = A^c
  • C \setminus (A \cup B) = (C \setminus A) \cap (C \setminus B)
  • C \setminus (A \cap B) = (C \setminus A) \cup (C \setminus B)

Symmetric difference:

  • A \triangle B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)
  • A \triangle B = (A \cup B) \setminus (A \cap B)
  • A \triangle B = B \triangle A
  • (A \triangle B) \triangle C = A \triangle (B \triangle C)
  • A \triangle \emptyset = A, A \triangle A = \emptyset
  • A \triangle B = \emptyset \iff A = B
Intuition

The two "C \setminus" rules are De Morgan inside C: removing "A or B" from C leaves what is outside A and outside B. And A \triangle B = \emptyset \iff A = B says "no element lies in exactly one of them", i.e. every element is in both or neither — which is equality.

How to prove set identities

To prove X = Y, show that they contain exactly the same elements: take an arbitrary element x, then compare the statements x \in X and x \in Y.

Typical proof structure:

x \in X \iff \text{logical statement} \iff x \in Y
Symbols
  • X, Y — the two set expressions to be shown equal (e.g. X = (A \cup B)^c, Y = A^c \cap B^c)
  • x — an arbitrary element of U: nothing is assumed about it, so the argument covers every element

Set identities are often logic identities in disguise.

Board: two ways to prove X = Y.

  1. Elementwise: x \in X \iff \cdots \iff x \in Y.
  2. Or prove both inclusions: X \subseteq Y and Y \subseteq X.

Board example: prove A \cup B = B \cup A. For arbitrary x,

x \in A \cup B \iff (x \in A) \vee (x \in B) \iff (x \in B) \vee (x \in A) \iff x \in B \cup A
Symbols
  • \vee — "or"; the middle step uses that \vee is commutative in logic

Hence A \cup B = B \cup A. Also on the board: A \cap U = A and A \cup U = U (picture: A inside U).

Board example of a set identity: A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C). For arbitrary x \in U,

\begin{aligned} x \in A \setminus (B \cup C) &\iff (x \in A) \wedge (x \notin B \cup C) \\ &\iff (x \in A) \wedge (x \notin B) \wedge (x \notin C) \\ &\iff \big[(x \in A) \wedge (x \notin B)\big] \wedge \big[(x \in A) \wedge (x \notin C)\big] \\ &\iff (x \in A \setminus B) \wedge (x \in A \setminus C) \\ &\iff x \in (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • A, B, C \subseteq U; \wedge — "and"; x \notin B \cup C — "x is in neither B nor C" (De Morgan)
  • line 3 writes x \in A twice, which is allowed because P \wedge P \iff P
Common mistake — "I drew the Venn diagram, so it's proved"

A Venn diagram shows one arrangement of the sets, and a check with concrete sets (like the board's \{0\}, \{1,2\}, \{2,3\} example below) shows the identity holds once. Neither covers every possible A, B, C. A proof starts with "Let x be arbitrary" and follows the logic, or proves both inclusions. Diagrams and examples are for finding and illustrating an identity — and one counterexample is enough to refute one.

Example proof: one De Morgan law

We prove (A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c. For arbitrary x \in U,

\begin{aligned} x \in (A \cup B)^c &\iff x \notin A \cup B \\ &\iff \neg(x \in A \text{ or } x \in B) \\ &\iff x \notin A \text{ and } x \notin B \\ &\iff x \in A^c \text{ and } x \in B^c \\ &\iff x \in A^c \cap B^c \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • x \in U arbitrary; \neg — "not"; (\ldots)^c — complement in U

This is exactly \neg(P \vee Q) \iff (\neg P \wedge \neg Q).

Worked example — proving C \setminus (A \cap B) = (C \setminus A) \cup (C \setminus B) (slide 16)
  1. Fix an arbitrary element: let x \in U.
  2. Unfold the left side into logic: x \in C \setminus (A \cap B) \iff x \in C \wedge \neg(x \in A \wedge x \in B).
  3. Apply De Morgan inside: \iff x \in C \wedge (x \notin A \vee x \notin B).
  4. Distribute \wedge over \vee: \iff (x \in C \wedge x \notin A) \vee (x \in C \wedge x \notin B).
  5. Fold back into sets: \iff x \in C \setminus A \ \vee\ x \in C \setminus B \iff x \in (C \setminus A) \cup (C \setminus B).
  6. Sanity check with numbers (illustration, not proof): C = \{1, \ldots, 6\}, A = \{2, 4, 6, 8\}, B = \{3, 6, 9\}: A \cap B = \{6\}, so the left side is \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}; C \setminus A = \{1, 3, 5\}, C \setminus B = \{1, 2, 4, 5\}, union \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\} ✓.

Cartesian product

The Cartesian product of A and B is the set of ordered pairs

A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\}
Symbols
  • (a, b) — ordered pair: first coordinate a, second coordinate b
  • A \times B — the set of all such pairs with first coordinate from A and second from B (read "A cross B")

If A = \{1, 2, 3\}, B = \{1, 2, 5\}, then A \times B contains 3 \cdot 3 = 9 ordered pairs.

\lvert A \times B \rvert = \lvert A \rvert \cdot \lvert B \rvert \quad \text{for finite sets}
Symbols
  • \lvert \cdot \rvert — cardinality (number of elements); A, B finite

A \times B for A = \{1, 2, 3\}, B = \{1, 2, 5\}: one grid point per ordered pair (a, b) (slide 19).

Board. A set does not remember order: \{a, b\} = \{b, a\}. An ordered pair does: (a, b) \neq (b, a) in general. (Picture: the point (x, y) in the x-y plane.)

Intuition

The grid on the slide is the whole idea: A along one axis, B along the other, one point per combination. Rows times columns gives \lvert A \rvert \cdot \lvert B \rvert. With A = B = \mathbb{R} the grid fills the whole plane: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^2 is exactly the coordinate plane, and a point is an ordered pair of real numbers.

Card example

Let R = \{A, K, Q, J\} and S = \{\spadesuit, \heartsuit, \diamondsuit, \clubsuit\}. R \times S is the set of cards with these ranks and suits: first choose a rank, then choose a suit — all rank–suit combinations (4 \cdot 4 = 16 cards: A♠ K♠ Q♠ J♠, A♡ K♡ Q♡ J♡, A♢ K♢ Q♢ J♢, A♣ K♣ Q♣ J♣). (Here A is the ace, not a set.)

Order matters

In general, A \times B \neq B \times A. For example, let A = \{1, 2\}, B = \{a, b\}:

  • A \times B = \{(1, a), (1, b), (2, a), (2, b)\},
  • B \times A = \{(a, 1), (a, 2), (b, 1), (b, 2)\}.

An ordered pair remembers which coordinate came first.

Board example: A = \{1, 2\}, B = \{1, 2, 3\}: A \times B = \{(1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (2,2), (2,3)\}, B \times A = \{(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2), (3,1), (3,2)\}. Thus A \times B \neq B \times A in general, and for finite sets \lvert A \times B \rvert = \lvert A \rvert \lvert B \rvert.

Common mistake — treating (a, b) like \{a, b\}

Tempting: "A \times B and B \times A have the same pairs, just written the other way round." In the board example both have 6 elements, but (1, 3) \in A \times B while (1, 3) \notin B \times A (there the first coordinate comes from B and the second from A = \{1, 2\}, which has no 3). Same size, different sets. A \times B = B \times A only in special cases, e.g. A = B or one of them empty.

Cartesian product: properties

  • A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)
  • A \times (B \cup C) = (A \times B) \cup (A \times C)
  • A \times (B \setminus C) = (A \times B) \setminus (A \times C)
  • (A \cap B) \times (C \cap D) = (A \times C) \cap (B \times D)
  • (A \times B) \times C \neq A \times (B \times C) in general: the nesting of ordered pairs is different.

For most applications, the important idea is: Cartesian products describe all combinations of choices.

Board check of the first property. Let A = \{0\}, B = \{1, 2\}, C = \{2, 3\}. Then B \cap C = \{2\} and A \times (B \cap C) = \{(0, 2)\}. Also A \times B = \{(0, 1), (0, 2)\}, A \times C = \{(0, 2), (0, 3)\}, so (A \times B) \cap (A \times C) = \{(0, 2)\}. Both sides agree in this example.

Why does A \times (B \cup C) = (A \times B) \cup (A \times C) hold for all sets?

Elements of these sets are pairs, so take an arbitrary pair (x, y): (x, y) \in A \times (B \cup C) \iff x \in A \wedge (y \in B \vee y \in C) \iff (x \in A \wedge y \in B) \vee (x \in A \wedge y \in C) (distributive law of logic) \iff (x, y) \in A \times B \ \vee\ (x, y) \in A \times C \iff (x, y) \in (A \times B) \cup (A \times C). Same method as before; only the "arbitrary element" is now a pair. Replace \vee by \wedge and you get the \cap rule.

Connection

"All combinations of choices" is how robotics describes a robot's possible states. A 2-joint planar arm (as in Introduction to Robotics, 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics) has joint space [0, 2\pi) \times [0, 2\pi): one angle for each joint, every combination allowed. Its configuration space is that product, and slide 3's "state spaces and configuration spaces" are built this way.

Board: families of sets

Let A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n be sets.

Intersection of many sets:

\bigcap_{k=1}^{n} A_k = A_1 \cap A_2 \cap \cdots \cap A_n = \{x : x \in A_k \text{ for all } k = 1, \ldots, n\}
Symbols
  • A_1, \ldots, A_n — a family of n sets, numbered by the index k
  • \bigcap_{k=1}^{n} A_k — the intersection of all A_k, k = 1, \ldots, n: elements lying in every A_k

Union of many sets:

\bigcup_{k=1}^{n} A_k = A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_n = \{x : x \in A_k \text{ for some } k\}
Symbols
  • \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} A_k — the union of all A_k: elements lying in at least one A_k ("for some k"); other symbols as above

Cartesian product:

\prod_{k=1}^{n} A_k = A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) : x_k \in A_k \text{ for } k = 1, \ldots, n\}
Symbols
  • \prod_{k=1}^{n} A_k — the Cartesian product of A_1, \ldots, A_n (here \prod means "product of sets", not multiplication of numbers)
  • (x_1, \ldots, x_n) — an ordered n-tuple: n coordinates in a fixed order, the k-th one from A_k

If all sets are the same, A^n = A \times A \times \cdots \times A (n factors).

Big symbols are shorthand, for comparison \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k = a_1 + \cdots + a_n. Similarly \bigcup, \bigcap and \prod collect repeated operations compactly.

Intuition

"For all k" for \bigcap and "for some k" for \bigcup are the quantifiers \forall and \exists from chapter 1: the big intersection is a big "and", the big union a big "or". \mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{R} is the set of vectors with n real components from 2.1 Linear Algebra Fundamentals.

Summary

Basic language

  • set, element, membership;
  • subset, equality, cardinality;
  • empty set, power set.

Operations: A^c, A \cap B, A \cup B, A \setminus B, A \triangle B.

Structure

  • set identities can be proved elementwise;
  • Cartesian products give ordered combinations;
  • sets of real numbers have bounds;
  • max / min must belong to the set, while sup / inf need not.

Key Facts

Language

  • x \in A, x \notin A
  • A \subseteq B; A = B \iff A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A
  • \lvert A \rvert = number of elements of A (finite A)

Set operations

  • A^c, A \cap B, A \cup B, A \setminus B, A \triangle B
  • A \triangle B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)
  • (A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c
  • (A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c

Products and proofs

  • A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}
  • For finite sets, \lvert A \times B \rvert = \lvert A \rvert \, \lvert B \rvert.
  • To prove X = Y, show x \in X \iff x \in Y for arbitrary x.

Special sets and power set

  • \emptyset \subseteq A for every set A.
  • \mathcal{P}(A) = \{B : B \subseteq A\}.
  • For finite A, \lvert \mathcal{P}(A) \rvert = 2^{\lvert A \rvert}.
  • \lvert \emptyset \rvert = 0, \lvert \{\emptyset\} \rvert = 1.
